Quick summary of what the infra team found from initial triage (timeline below). Full dump attached (netdiag-20270207.txt).

Findings:
- Between 07:48–08:55 PST we observed frequent BGP withdraw/announce events on the dedicated interconnect to Acme's VPC — the peer reported multiple route flap events.
- SNAT port utilization spiked concurrently; many short-lived TCP connections recreated SNAT tuples which exhausted ephemeral port availability on the NAT gateway pool for the dedicated capacity.
- With SNAT exhaustion the gateway started returning 429 for new connections; application retries triggered 5xx from downstream microservices due to connection timeouts and queue pressure.
- Firewall connection-tracking (conntrack) entries also reached high-water marks causing additional drops.

Immediate mitigations we applied (10:05–10:30 PST):
1) Increased ephemeral SNAT port range and added an extra NAT node to the dedicated pool (temporary scaling).
2) Implemented a connection-aging policy to prune conntrack entries more aggressively for this customer route.
3) Opened a temporary policy to route 25% of Acme's traffic to our hosted cluster (fall-back) to reduce pressure and give us headroom for a controlled rollout.

Next steps:
- Continue monitoring BGP stability on the peer; we suspect intermittent peering flap on Acme's end or intermediate cloud fabric. We have asked Acme to check their peering.
- If flaps persist, recommend a long-term fix: increase HA across NAT devices and implement per-customer SNAT isolation for high-churn workloads.

Attachment: netdiag-20270207.txt (summary + counters)

-Vivek

Subject: Exec summary & short-term remediation — Acme Retail incident

Lauren — quick executive summary and the actions we've taken so far. I'm copying our head of account (Marissa) and ops head (Hannah) so you have direct escalation contacts.

What happened:
- Starting ~07:48 PST Acme-dedicated traffic experienced route flaps on the peering which coincided with excessive SNAT churn and conntrack saturation on the dedicated NAT pool. This caused elevated 429 responses for new outbound connections and cascading 5xx errors from backend retries.

What we did immediately:
- Scaled NAT capacity and bumped ephemeral port range to reduce exhaustion.
- Applied more aggressive conntrack pruning and tuned TCP timeouts.
- Shifted ~25% of traffic to our hosted fallback to relieve pressure while we monitor.
- Kept a small canary on the dedicated path to validate improvements.

Current status (14:15 PST):
- 5xx/429 rates have dropped ~80% compared to the peak. Latency is trending back to normal for the canary traffic.
- We're still seeing occasional BGP withdraw events; we've asked Acme's network team to validate their peering fabric and to check for flaps in their cloud provider region.

Proposed next steps / ask from Acme:
1) Can your network team confirm if they observed route instability on their side between 07:40–09:00 PST?
2) Approve a temporary 25% permanent failover window (we keep traffic on hosted fallback during business hours for 48 hours) while both teams stabilize peering.
3) We'll schedule a post-incident call tomorrow with our networking leads to walk the trace and plan a durable fix (per-customer SNAT isolation and additional NAT HA).

Credits / customer impact: we understand this caused revenue-impacting latency for checkout personalization. Marissa will lead the commercial conversation on credits once we have a full scope (estimated affected requests).

I'll escalate to execs if the route flaps continue beyond today — want to avoid surprises for Acme.

Apologies again to the team — we're prioritizing this.

Best,
Avery Johnson
